claim: Pericentromeric satellite DNA repeats are ubiquitous and abundant in eukaryotes.
source: A central principle underlying the ubiquity and abundance of pericentromeric satellite DNA repeats in eukaryotes has remained poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as established background in the abstract.

claim: Interchromosomal clustering of satellite DNAs into chromocenters ensures encapsulation of all chromosomes into a single nucleus.
source: Previously we proposed that the interchromosomal clustering of satellite DNAs into nuclear structures known as chromocenters ensures encapsulation of all chromosomes into a single nucleus (Jagannathan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Chromocenter disruption leads to micronuclei formation, resulting in cell death.
source: Chromocenter disruption led to micronuclei formation, resulting in cell death.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work in the abstract.

claim: Chromocenter formation is mediated by a 'modular' network involving D1 and Prod proteins bound to their cognate satellite DNAs.
source: Here we show that chromocenter formation is mediated by a 'modular' network, where associations between two sequence-specific satellite DNA-binding proteins, D1 and Prod, bound to their cognate satellite DNAs, bring the full complement of chromosomes into the chromocenter.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: D1 prod double mutants die during embryogenesis.
source: D1 prod double mutants die during embryogenesis, exhibiting enhanced phenotypes associated with chromocenter disruption, revealing the universal importance of satellite DNAs and chromocenters.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing embryonic lethality in double mutants.

claim: Centromeric satellite DNA serves as a platform to form the kinetochore.
source: Whereas it is well established that centromeric satellite DNA serves as a platform to form the kinetochore (Sun et al., 1997; Sun et al., 2003; Willard, 1990), the role of pericentromeric heterochromatin has been obscure despite its abundance that surpasses far beyond centromeric heterochromatin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Satellite DNA has been repeatedly consigned to the status of genomic junk due to lack of protein-coding ability and lack of conservation among species.
source: Due to the lack of protein-coding ability and lack of conservation among species, satellite DNA has been repeatedly consigned to the status of genomic junk (Ohno, 1972; Orgel and Crick, 1980), even though they can constitute ~50% of eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: Satellite DNAs can constitute approximately 50% of eukaryotic genomes.
source: Due to the lack of protein-coding ability and lack of conservation among species, satellite DNA has been repeatedly consigned to the status of genomic junk (Ohno, 1972; Orgel and Crick, 1980), even though they can constitute ~50% of eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Pericentromeric satellite DNAs play a critical role in bundling multiple chromosomes, leading to the formation of chromocenters.
source: Our study indicated that pericentromeric satellite DNAs play a critical role in bundling multiple chromosomes, leading to the formation of 'chromocenters', cytological structures that have been recognized for ~100 years (Figure 1A) (Jones, 1970; Jost et al., 2012; Pardue and Gall, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and references to chromocenter structures.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster D1 bundles chromosomes by binding to the {AATAT}n satellite DNA.
source: We have shown that Drosophila melanogaster D1 and the mouse HMGA1 bundle chromosomes by binding to their cognate satellite DNAs ({AATAT}n and major satellite, respectively) and clustering them into chromocenters.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Mouse HMGA1 bundles chromosomes by binding to major satellite DNA.
source: We have shown that Drosophila melanogaster D1 and the mouse HMGA1 bundle chromosomes by binding to their cognate satellite DNAs ({AATAT}n and major satellite, respectively) and clustering them into chromocenters.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Loss of chromocenters due to mutation/depletion of satellite DNA-binding proteins results in the formation of micronuclei.
source: Loss of chromocenters (i.e. defective bundling of chromosomes) due to mutation/depletion of these satellite DNA-binding proteins resulted in the formation of micronuclei, because unbundled chromosomes budded out of interphase nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Micronuclei formation is associated with extensive DNA damage.
source: This was associated with extensive DNA damage, as has been observed with micronuclei in other systems (Crasta et al., 2012; Denais et al., 2016; Hatch et al., 2013; Raab et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on micronuclei and DNA damage.

claim: The {AATAT}n satellite is abundant on X, Y and 4th chromosomes in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: For example, in Drosophila melanogaster, the {AATAT}n satellite is abundant on X, Y and 4th chromosomes (Figure 1B), and we have shown that the D1 protein, which recognizes this satellite DNA, plays a critical role in chromocenter formation.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Chromosome 2 possesses little if any of the {AATAT}n satellite DNA.
source: However, chromosome 2 possesses little if any of the {AATAT}n satellite DNA (Figure 1B, arrowheads), and chromosome 3 possesses much less of this satellite DNA compared to X, Y and 4th chromosomes (Figure 1B, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Chromosome 3 possesses much less {AATAT}n satellite DNA compared to X, Y and 4th chromosomes.
source: However, chromosome 2 possesses little if any of the {AATAT}n satellite DNA (Figure 1B, arrowheads), and chromosome 3 possesses much less of this satellite DNA compared to X, Y and 4th chromosomes (Figure 1B, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA is abundantly present on chromosomes 2 and 3.
source: The {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA drew our attention, because it is abundantly present on chromosomes 2 and 3 (Figure 1B) and is known to be bound by the Proliferation disrupter (Prod) protein (Török et al., 1997; Török et al., 2000; Platero et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data in Figure 1B and citations to previous work.

claim: The {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA is bound by the Proliferation disrupter (Prod) protein.
source: The {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA drew our attention, because it is abundantly present on chromosomes 2 and 3 (Figure 1B) and is known to be bound by the Proliferation disrupter (Prod) protein (Török et al., 1997; Török et al., 2000; Platero et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA and Prod protein perfectly co-localize within interphase nuclei in multiple cell types.
source: Indeed, we observed that the {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA and Prod protein perfectly co-localized within interphase nuclei in multiple cell types such as spermatogonia, imaginal disc cells and lymph gland cells (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and FISH data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: The {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA exists at four loci in diploid cells (2 from 2nd, 2 from 3rd).
source: Whereas the {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA exists at four loci in diploid cells (2 from 2nd, 2 from 3rd) (Figure 1B), we predominantly observed two {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA foci per nucleus (Figure 1C–E), suggesting that this satellite DNA is bundled into chromocenters.
evidence: This is inferred from FISH data in Figure 1B showing the satellite on chromosomes 2 and 3.

claim: Two {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA foci are predominantly observed per nucleus.
source: Whereas the {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA exists at four loci in diploid cells (2 from 2nd, 2 from 3rd) (Figure 1B), we predominantly observed two {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA foci per nucleus (Figure 1C–E), suggesting that this satellite DNA is bundled into chromocenters.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: The number of {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA foci per nucleus significantly increases in cells depleted of Prod.
source: The number of {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA foci per nucleus significantly increased in cells depleted of Prod (both loss-of-function mutants and RNAi) (Figure 1F–K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting that Prod functions to bundle {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA into chromocenters.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F-K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Prod functions to bundle {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA into chromocenters.
source: The number of {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA foci per nucleus significantly increased in cells depleted of Prod (both loss-of-function mutants and RNAi) (Figure 1F–K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting that Prod functions to bundle {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA into chromocenters.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Prod depletion increases the number of satellite DNA foci.

claim: Loss-of-function of prod causes late larval lethality with atrophied imaginal discs and melanized lymph glands.
source: Loss-of-function of prod was reported to cause late larval lethality with these mutants containing atrophied imaginal discs and melanized lymph glands (Török et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mutation of prod results in the formation of micronuclei in larval imaginal discs and lymph glands.
source: Similar to these observations with D1 mutant germ cells, we observed that mutation of prod resulted in the formation of micronuclei in larval imaginal discs (Figure 2A–B,E) and lymph glands (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: More than 80% of micronuclei in prod mutants contain at least one of {AATAT}n or {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNAs.
source: These micronuclei almost always contained satellite DNA (Figure 2F, >80% of micronuclei contained at least one of {AATAT}n or {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNAs (n = 48)), supporting the idea that micronuclei formation is due to declustering of chromocenters.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2F with quantification.

claim: Micronuclei formation in prod mutants is due to declustering of chromocenters.
source: These micronuclei almost always contained satellite DNA (Figure 2F, >80% of micronuclei contained at least one of {AATAT}n or {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNAs (n = 48)), supporting the idea that micronuclei formation is due to declustering of chromocenters.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that micronuclei contain satellite DNA.

claim: When apoptotic cell death is blocked by expressing DIAP1, a striking increase in DNA damage is observed in prod mutant tissues.
source: However, when apoptotic cell death was blocked by expressing the death-associated inhibitor of apoptosis 1 (DIAP1) protein (Orme and Meier, 2009), we observed a striking increase in DNA damage in prod mutant tissues (Figure 2G–J), suggesting that prod mutation indeed increases DNA damage and that these damaged cells are rapidly cleared by apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by γ-H2Av staining data shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: Damaged cells in prod mutants are rapidly cleared by apoptosis.
source: However, when apoptotic cell death was blocked by expressing the death-associated inhibitor of apoptosis 1 (DIAP1) protein (Orme and Meier, 2009), we observed a striking increase in DNA damage in prod mutant tissues (Figure 2G–J), suggesting that prod mutation indeed increases DNA damage and that these damaged cells are rapidly cleared by apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DNA damage is only apparent when apoptosis is blocked.

claim: Germline depletion of prod results in disruption of {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA clustering.
source: Germline depletion of prod resulted in disruption of {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA clustering (Figure 1I–K) and defects in nuclear integrity: 27.9% of prod-depleted germ cells (n = 190) exhibited leakage of nls-GFP outside the major nucleus in comparison to 3.7% of control cells (n = 191) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1I-K.

claim: 27.9% of prod-depleted germ cells exhibit leakage of nls-GFP outside the major nucleus compared to 3.7% of control cells.
source: Germline depletion of prod resulted in disruption of {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA clustering (Figure 1I–K) and defects in nuclear integrity: 27.9% of prod-depleted germ cells (n = 190) exhibited leakage of nls-GFP outside the major nucleus in comparison to 3.7% of control cells (n = 191) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: D1 mutation results in severe micronuclei formation and cell death in the germline.
source: Conversely, D1 mutation, which results in severe micronuclei formation and cell death in the germline, did not show a significant increase in micronuclei formation in somatic tissues that are affected by prod mutation such as imaginal discs and lymph glands (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: D1 mutation does not show a significant increase in micronuclei formation in imaginal discs and lymph glands.
source: Conversely, D1 mutation, which results in severe micronuclei formation and cell death in the germline, did not show a significant increase in micronuclei formation in somatic tissues that are affected by prod mutation such as imaginal discs and lymph glands (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: D1 and prod exhibit synthetic lethality.
source: Despite the distinct tissue requirement of these genes, D1 prod double mutant exhibited synthetic lethality (see below) suggesting that these genes function in the same biological process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on double mutants presented later in the manuscript.

claim: D1 protein forms 'chromatin threads' that connect heterologous chromosomes.
source: Based on our previous observation that D1 protein forms 'chromatin threads' that connect heterologous chromosomes (Jagannathan et al., 2018), we postulated that these chromatin threads are the basis for chromocenter formation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Chromatin threads with Prod protein are observed.
source: Similarly, we observed chromatin threads with Prod protein (Figure 3A, arrowheads indicate two of the four Prod loci while the arrow indicates Prod threads connecting the two loci).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: D1/Prod-positive chromatin threads are only apparent during a narrow time window during mitotic prophase.
source: However, these D1/Prod-positive chromatin threads are only apparent during a narrow time window during mitotic prophase when individual chromosomes start to resolve from each other during chromosome condensation but prior to metaphase.
evidence: This is based on observations from microscopy experiments.

claim: By metaphase, the chromatin threads that connect heterologous chromosomes are completely resolved.
source: By metaphase, the chromatin threads that connect heterologous chromosomes were completely resolved, likely to allow mitotic chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is based on observations from microscopy experiments.

claim: Ectopic expression of GFP-Prod in spermatocytes leads to the formation of chromatin threads between heterologous chromosomes.
source: Strikingly, we found that ectopic expression of GFP-Prod in spermatocytes, which normally lack Prod (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), led to the formation of chromatin threads between heterologous chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Homologous chromosomes separate into distinct 'territories' within the nucleus in preparation of meiotic reductional division in spermatocytes of Drosophila.
source: It is well established that homologous chromosomes separate into distinct 'territories' within the nucleus in preparation of meiotic reductional division in spermatocytes of Drosophila (Figure 3B) (McKee, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Ectopic expression of GFP-tagged Prod protein in spermatocytes results in the formation of chromatin threads between distinct chromosome territories.
source: Ectopic expression of GFP-tagged Prod protein in spermatocytes resulted in the formation of chromatin threads between distinct chromosome territories (Figure 3C) with these bridges positive for both Prod protein and the {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA (Figure 3C, arrows indicate Prod-{AATAACATAG}n threads connecting chromosome territories marked by the yellow dashed lines).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and FISH data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The two chromosomal territories connected by ectopically expressed Prod are territories containing chromosomes 2 and 3.
source: The two chromosomal territories connected by ectopically expressed Prod are territories containing chromosomes 2 and 3, as determined by FISH using 2nd and 3rd chromosome specific probes ({AACAC}n satellite for 2, dodeca satellite for 3) (Jagannathan et al., 2017) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3D using chromosome-specific probes.

claim: Ectopically expressed Prod binds the {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA on chromosomes 2 and 3, and physically links these chromosomes.
source: These data clearly demonstrate that ectopically expressed Prod bound the {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA on chromosomes 2 and 3, and physically linked these chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH and microscopy data showing Prod-positive threads connecting chromosome territories.

claim: Prod is sufficient to bundle heterologous chromosomes via binding its cognate satellite DNA, {AATAACATAG}n.
source: We conclude that Prod is sufficient to bundle heterologous chromosomes via binding its cognate satellite DNA, {AATAACATAG}n, providing a mechanistic explanation how chromocenters are formed by bundling of specific satellite DNA sequences located on heterologous chromosomes.
evidence: This is concluded from the ectopic expression experiments showing Prod can link chromosomes.

claim: D1 and Prod were predicted to interact with each other, albeit weakly, based on a high-throughput mass spectrometry screen in Schneider S2 cells.
source: We noted that D1 and Prod were predicted to interact with each other, albeit weakly, based on a high-throughput mass spectrometry screen in Schneider S2 cells (Guruharsha et al., 2011), suggesting that satellite DNA bundled by D1 and that bundled by Prod might further cluster together via an interaction between Prod and D1 proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a mass spectrometry study.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments did not detect any physical interaction between D1 and Prod proteins.
source: However, co-immunoprecipitation experiments did not detect any physical interaction between these proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that their interaction may be weak or transient.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: D1- and Prod-positive foci are consistently juxtaposed within the heterochromatic domain of the nucleus.
source: We observed that D1- and Prod-positive foci were consistently juxtaposed within the heterochromatic domain of the nucleus (Figure 4A, the heterochromatic domain is demarcated by the yellow dashed line and is based on HP1 localization).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: D1 and Prod foci are not static but rather move dynamically within the nucleus.
source: While we have observed an average of ~4–5 D1-positive foci/nucleus and ~2 Prod positive foci/nucleus in fixed and stained samples, the live observation demonstrated that these foci are not static but rather moving dynamically within the nucleus (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: D1 and Prod exhibit similar diffusion coefficients.
source: Using single particle tracking, we estimated the diffusion coefficient (D), which indicated that D1 and Prod exhibited similar dynamics (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The majority of D1 and Prod foci exhibit SMSS <0.5, suggesting confined motion.
source: The majority of D1 and Prod foci exhibited SMSS <0.5 (Figure 4E), suggesting confined motion, likely within the heterochromatin domain.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: D1-positive foci and Prod-positive foci frequently become juxtaposed in a 'kiss and run' manner.
source: D1-positive foci and Prod-positive foci frequently became juxtaposed in a 'kiss and run' manner: coming into contact temporarily and separating from each other soon after (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Chromocenter is a structure comprised of dynamic modules of satellite DNAs and satellite DNA binding proteins, rather than rigidly linked satellite DNAs.
source: These results indicate that chromocenter is a structure comprised of dynamic modules of satellite DNAs and satellite DNA binding proteins, rather than rigidly linked satellite DNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the dynamic behavior of D1 and Prod foci observed in live imaging.

claim: The dynamism exhibited by satellite DNA binding proteins may reflect the liquid droplet-like properties of heterochromatin.
source: The dynamism exhibited by these satellite DNA binding proteins may reflect the recently demonstrated liquid droplet-like properties of heterochromatin (Larson et al., 2017; Strom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on citations to recent work on heterochromatin properties.

claim: Mutation of prod results in defective clustering of D1 protein within the nuclei of imaginal discs, neuroblasts and spermatogonial germ cells.
source: Indeed, we found that mutation of prod resulted in defective clustering of D1 protein within the nuclei of imaginal discs, neuroblasts and spermatogonial germ cells (Figure 4H–J and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4H-J and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-I.

claim: Mutation of D1 results in the disruption of Prod protein clustering in multiple tissues.
source: Similarly, mutation of D1 resulted in the disruption of Prod protein clustering in multiple tissues (Figure 4K–M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–O).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4K-M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2J-O.

claim: FISH experiments confirm the declustering of {AATAT}n in prod mutant, and that of {AATAACATAG}n in D1 mutant cells.
source: FISH experiments confirmed the declustering of {AATAT}n in prod mutant, and that of {AATAACATAG}n in D1 mutant cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–H).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-H.

claim: Modules of Prod, D1 and their cognate satellite DNA function in a mutually dependent manner to form chromocenters.
source: Taken together, these results support the idea that modules of Prod, D1 and their cognate satellite DNA function in a mutually dependent manner to form chromocenters.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual dependency observed in clustering experiments.

claim: The inter-dependency of D1 and Prod shapes a network-like configuration for chromocenters and forms the basis for bundling the 'entire set' of chromosomes.
source: We propose that this inter-dependency shapes a network-like configuration for chromocenters and forms the basis for bundling the 'entire set' of chromosomes, instead of bundling individual satellite DNAs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed mutual dependency.

claim: D1 and prod double mutants (GFP-negative animals) are underrepresented in larval population.
source: We observed that D1 and prod double mutants (i.e. GFP-negative animals) were underrepresented (far below expected frequency at 6.25%) in larval population in contrast to GFP-negative larvae from control parents (+/CyO, Act-GFP; +/TM3, Act-GFP) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Double mutant animals largely fail to develop past the embryo stage.
source: These data suggested that double mutant animals largely failed to develop past the embryo stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the underrepresentation of double mutants in larval populations.

claim: 7.6% of embryos from mated D1 and prod heterozygote parents exhibit abnormal development.
source: A closer examination revealed that 7.6% of embryos from mated D1 and prod heterozygote parents exhibited abnormal development, (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Micronuclei are observed in defective embryos from D1 and prod heterozygote parents.
source: We observed micronuclei in these defective embryos (Figure 5D–E) as well as numerous extranuclear DAPI-intense foci (Figure 5E, arrows), which we suggest is the terminal phenotype of cells with micronuclei due to chromocenter disruption.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Extranuclear DAPI-intense foci are the terminal phenotype of cells with micronuclei due to chromocenter disruption.
source: We observed micronuclei in these defective embryos (Figure 5D–E) as well as numerous extranuclear DAPI-intense foci (Figure 5E, arrows), which we suggest is the terminal phenotype of cells with micronuclei due to chromocenter disruption.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation of extranuclear DAPI foci in defective embryos.

claim: Satellite DNA abundance is remarkably stable over multiple generations.
source: Nonetheless, satellite DNA abundance is remarkably stable over multiple generations, despite being prone to copy number loss through mechanisms such as replicative slippage and intrachromatid exchange (Charlesworth et al., 1994), implying that satellite DNA must serve unappreciated function(s).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Satellite DNA is prone to copy number loss through mechanisms such as replicative slippage and intrachromatid exchange.
source: Nonetheless, satellite DNA abundance is remarkably stable over multiple generations, despite being prone to copy number loss through mechanisms such as replicative slippage and intrachromatid exchange (Charlesworth et al., 1994), implying that satellite DNA must serve unappreciated function(s).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Drosophila melanogaster genome contains at least 17 satellite DNAs.
source: Given that the Drosophila melanogaster genome contains at least 17 satellite DNAs (Jagannathan et al., 2017; Lohe et al., 1993), it is plausible that additional satellite DNA binding proteins may participate in chromocenter formation, even though D1 and Prod can cover the full complement of D. melanogaster chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Additional satellite DNA binding proteins may participate in chromocenter formation.
source: Given that the Drosophila melanogaster genome contains at least 17 satellite DNAs (Jagannathan et al., 2017; Lohe et al., 1993), it is plausible that additional satellite DNA binding proteins may participate in chromocenter formation, even though D1 and Prod can cover the full complement of D. melanogaster chromosomes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the number of satellite DNAs in the genome.

claim: The 17 satellite DNAs might reflect the history of the species, wherein individual satellites were essential at some point, while only a subset are critically important for the present day D. melanogaster genome.
source: Alternatively, these 17 satellite DNAs might reflect the history of the species, wherein individual satellites were essential at some point, while only a subset are critically important for the present day D. melanogaster genome.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the evolutionary history of satellite DNAs.

claim: The association of satellite DNA binding proteins can form a chromocenter network, thereby packaging the entire genome within a single nucleus.
source: We further suggest that the association of satellite DNA binding proteins can form a chromocenter network, thereby packaging the entire genome within a single nucleus.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed interactions between D1 and Prod.

claim: While cells can compensate for the loss of an individual chromocenter module, loss of multiple chromocenter modules will result in more widespread and penetrant cellular defects.
source: This suggests that while cells can compensate for the loss of an individual chromocenter module, loss of multiple chromocenter modules will result in more widespread and penetrant cellular defects, illuminating an essential function for chromocenter formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the synthetic lethality observed in double mutants.

claim: The essence of satellite DNA function is to be bound by sequence-specific binding proteins that have the ability to bundle these repeats into chromocenters.
source: Our data suggest that the essence of satellite DNA function is to be bound by sequence-specific binding proteins that have the ability to bundle these repeats into chromocenters.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The satellite DNA sequence itself does not need to be conserved.
source: As such, the satellite DNA sequence itself does not need to be conserved.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed model of satellite DNA function.

claim: The {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA is completely absent in Drosophila simulans.
source: For instance, the {AATAACATAG}n satellite DNA, which is a central player in bundling the Drosophila melanogaster major autosomes, is completely absent in its nearest relative, Drosophila simulans.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about satellite DNA divergence between species.

claim: If satellite DNA repeats diverge rapidly, their binding proteins will also likely adapt to attain optimal binding specificity for the diverged sequences.
source: These observations lead to an interesting speculation: if satellite DNA repeats diverge rapidly, their binding proteins will also likely adapt to attain optimal binding specificity for the diverged sequences.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about co-evolution of satellite DNAs and their binding proteins.

claim: Divergence in satellite DNA sequences and their binding proteins may lead to incompatibility in chromocenter formation when chromosomes from D. melanogaster and D. simulans are brought together in hybrids.
source: It is tempting to speculate that such divergence in satellite DNA sequences and their binding proteins may lead to incompatibility in chromocenter formation when chromosomes from these two species are brought together in hybrids.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential hybrid incompatibility.

claim: Satellite DNA and their binding proteins conform to a modular system, whereby all the chromosomes are brought into a chromocenter network by the association of satellite DNA binding proteins.
source: In summary, we propose that satellite DNA and their binding proteins conform to a modular system, whereby all the chromosomes are brought into a chromocenter network by the association of satellite DNA binding proteins.
evidence: This is the main proposed model summarizing the findings of the study.

claim: Chromocenter plays a fundamental role in securing all the chromosomes within a single nucleus.
source: In this manner, chromocenter plays a fundamental role in securing all the chromosomes within a single nucleus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.
